extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and beginning graduate students studying measure theory / Lebesgue integration
extracted.subtask_description: Detailed textbook exposition proving the Extension Theorem (construction/uniqueness of measure extensions from an algebra/σ‑ring, inner/outer measures, completion) and introductory steps toward Fubini's Theorem (product σ‑algebra, sections, measurability of section measures and iterated integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 5.31 (bounded dominated convergence special case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E has finite measure, c ∈ R, and {f_n} is a sequence of measurable functions with |f_n| ≤ c for all n and f_n → f pointwise, then lim_n ∫_E f_n dµ exists, f is integrable on E, and ∫_E f dµ = lim_n ∫_E f_n dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the special case of dominated convergence when the dominating function g is the constant c; invoked as an immediate corollary of the general dominated convergence theorem (Theorem 5.30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of outer and inner measures µ* and µ_* via U and K
rubrics_metrics.description: For an algebra A, let U be the class of countable unions of sets in A and K the class of countable intersections of sets in A. Define for arbitrary E ⊆ X: µ*(E) = inf_{U ∈ U, U ⊇ E} µ*(U) (outer measure) and µ_*(E) = sup_{K ∈ K, K ⊆ E} µ_*(K) (inner measure), where µ* and µ_* on U and K are defined by appropriate limiting procedures from ∫ on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: µ* and µ_* extend the original set function ∫: on U (increasing unions) and K (decreasing intersections) they are defined by limits of ∫(A_n) for sequences in A; these are the basic upper and lower bounds used to define the extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 5.32 (properties of µ* and µ_* on U and K)
rubrics_metrics.description: For U an increasing union of A_n in A and K a decreasing intersection of C_n in A, µ*(U) = lim ∫(A_n) and µ_*(K) = lim ∫(C_n). Properties: (a) µ* and µ_* agree with ∫ on A; (b) monotonicity: if U ⊆ V in U then µ*(U) ≤ µ*(V); (c) µ_* respects decreasing intersections in K; (d) µ* respects increasing unions in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limit definitions and properties ensure µ* and µ_* are well-defined on the larger classes U and K and behave like measures under monotone sequences; proofs use propositions on limits of integrals and set-function continuity on A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and (countable) additivity/subadditivity of µ* and µ_* (Lemma 5.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊆ B then µ*(A) ≤ µ*(B) and µ_*(A) ≤ µ_*(B). Moreover: (a) if E ⊆ ⋃_n E_n then µ*(E) ≤ Σ_n µ*(E_n) (countable subadditivity for outer measure); (b) if F and G are disjoint then µ_*(F ∪ G) = µ_*(F) + µ_*(G) (finite additivity of inner measure on disjoint sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity follows because the infimum/supremum defining µ*/µ_* range over larger/smaller classes; the subadditivity and additivity statements are proved first on approximating sequences from A and then extended to arbitrary sets by approximation and limiting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality µ_*(E) ≤ µ*(E) and equality on U or K (Lemma 5.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every subset E of X one has µ_*(E) ≤ µ*(E). Equality holds when E lies in U or in K (i.e., for sets obtained as countable unions/intersections from the algebra A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inequality is fundamental: when inner and outer measures coincide the set has a well-defined measure equal to that common value; U and K are classes where the two constructions agree because of the limit definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of measurable sets for the extension procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset E of X is defined to be measurable (for the extension) if µ_*(E) = µ*(E). Let B denote the class of such measurable sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 5.34 shows that the algebra A and the classes U and K are contained in B. The measurable sets B will (and should) form the σ‑algebra on which the extended measure is defined by assigning µ(E) := µ*(E)=µ_*(E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation of measurable sets by U and K (Lemma 5.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ∈ U and K ∈ K with K ⊆ U then µ*(U  ackslash K) = µ*(U) − µ_*(K). If E is measurable, then for any ε>0 there exist K ∈ K and U ∈ U with K ⊆ E ⊆ U and µ*(U  ackslash K) ≤ ε (i.e., inner and outer approximations can be made arbitrarily close).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the standard inner/outer regularity approximation: measurable sets can be sandwiched between K and U whose measures differ by arbitrarily small amount, used repeatedly in proving closure properties and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class of measurable sets is a σ‑algebra and µ* restricts to a measure (Lemma 5.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class B of measurable sets is a σ‑algebra containing the original algebra A, and the restriction of µ* to B is a measure (completely additive set function) extending ∫ on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof proceeds by verifying closure under complements, finite intersections, and countable disjoint unions using the approximations from K and U and the properties of µ*/µ_* established earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of measure extension in finite total measure case (Theorem 5.5 special case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an algebra on X and ∫ is a nonnegative completely additive set function on A with ∫(X) finite, then there exists a unique measure µ on the smallest σ‑algebra containing A extending ∫; the extension is obtained by constructing µ* and restricting to measurable sets B where µ_*=µ*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence: define µ* and B as above and show B is σ‑algebra and µ*|_B extends ∫. Uniqueness: any other extension µ0 must agree with µ* on approximating K and U sets, hence on their supremum/infimum limits and therefore on all measurable sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension under σ‑finiteness (general case of Theorem 5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the given ring R (or algebra) has a nonnegative completely additive set function ∫ that is σ‑finite, then ∫ extends uniquely to a measure on the smallest σ‑ring/σ‑algebra containing R: partition X into a countable union of sets with finite ∫, extend on each piece (finite case), and paste the extensions together consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: for each piece S with ∫(S) finite, extend uniquely to a σ‑algebra on S; check consistency of these piecewise measures on overlaps and define µ(E) by choosing a containing S and taking the previously defined µ_S(E). Complete additivity and uniqueness follow from consistency and σ‑finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical extension from a σ‑ring to the smallest σ‑algebra (Proposition 5.37)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a σ‑ring R, let Rc be the class of complements of members of R. Either R = Rc = A (so R already is a σ‑algebra) or A = R ∪ Rc is the smallest σ‑algebra containing R. In the latter case any measure µ on R has a canonical extension µ1 to A given by µ1(E) = sup{µ(F) : F ∈ R, F ⊆ E} for E ∈ A, and any other extension µ2 satisfies µ2 ≥ µ1 on A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The result gives an explicit canonical way to extend a measure defined on a σ‑ring to the generated σ‑algebra by taking suprema over R-subsets (and shows this is minimal among extensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of a measure space (definition and Proposition 5.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: The completion of (X, A, µ) is the σ‑algebra A' = {E ∪ Z : E ∈ A, Z ⊆ Z0 for some Z0 ∈ A with µ(Z0) = 0} equipped with µ(E ∪ Z) := µ(E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 5.38 details: (a) A' is a σ‑algebra containing A; (b) µ is unambiguously defined on A'; (c) µ is a measure on A'; (d) the completion is complete (every subset of a null set is measurable); (e) when µ(X) < ∞, A' can be characterized in terms of outer/inner measures: E ∈ A' iff µ*(E) = µ_*(E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of null sets in R1 (Proposition 5.39)
rubrics_metrics.description: In R^1, Lebesgue measurable sets of measure zero are exactly the subsets E that for every ε>0 can be covered by countably many intervals whose total length is less than ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the classical characterization of null sets via interval covers (outer measure via countable unions of intervals); proof reduces to bounded intervals then uses countable covering and a diagonal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product σ‑algebra and measurable rectangles (definition and Proposition 5.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given σ‑algebras A on X and B on Y, the product σ‑algebra A × B is the smallest σ‑algebra containing all measurable rectangles A × B (A ∈ A, B ∈ B). The algebra C of finite disjoint unions of measurable rectangles is an algebra (closed under finite unions, complements, intersections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebra C is used as the generating algebra for the product σ‑algebra; complements of rectangles decompose into finite unions of rectangles, ensuring C is an algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections of sets and their measurability (definition and Proposition 5.42)
rubrics_metrics.description: For E ⊆ X × Y and x ∈ X define the section E_x = {y ∈ Y : (x,y) ∈ E}; for y ∈ Y define E^y = {x ∈ X : (x,y) ∈ E}. If E is measurable in the product σ‑algebra A × B then each section E_x ∈ B and each E^y ∈ A (sections are measurable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show the class of sets with measurable sections is a σ‑algebra containing the rectangles (since rectangle sections are either empty or a side), hence contains A × B. This is used in forming iterated integrals where the inner integral is ∫(E_x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone Class Lemma (Lemma 5.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallest monotone class (closed under countable increasing unions and countable decreasing intersections) containing an algebra A coincides with the smallest σ‑algebra containing A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is the technical tool to pass from an algebra to the σ‑algebra by showing the minimal monotone class already contains finite unions and complements; it is used in the product/section measurability arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability of x ↦ ∫(E_x) and y ↦ µ(E^y) under σ‑finiteness (Lemma 5.44)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X,A,µ) and (Y,B,∫) are σ‑finite measure spaces, then for every measurable E ⊆ X × Y the functions x ↦ ∫(E_x) and y ↦ µ(E^y) are measurable (with respect to A and B respectively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: first treat finite measure spaces by showing the class of E with measurable section-measure functions contains the algebra of finite unions of rectangles and is a monotone class; then reduce the σ‑finite case by partitioning into countably many finite-measure pieces and summing contributions (countable sums of measurable functions are measurable). This measurability is the crucial step before applying Fubini.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy for Fubini’s Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove equality of iterated integrals for integrable nonnegative (or integrable) f on X × Y: (i) prove the identity for indicator functions of measurable sets (hard step: measurability of section integrals); (ii) extend to simple functions by linearity; (iii) pass to limits via Monotone Convergence to cover nonnegative measurable functions and then absolute integrability for the general case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that the main technical difficulty is step (i): showing x ↦ ∫(E_x) is measurable. Once that is secured (via monotone class arguments and σ‑finiteness), the rest follows by standard measure-theoretic limit arguments.
